name: Prahlad Gaitonde
role: Computer Science Undergraduate — Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning

hero.line: From neuron to network — I train models, publish what they find, and build the interfaces that explain them.
hero.lede: Computer Science undergraduate at **Manipal Institute of Technology**, specialising in AI & ML. Published IEEE author. Currently: dynamic relation weighting for sequential recommenders.

neuron.caption: Pyramidal neuron — soma, dendritic arbour, axon. After Cajal, 1899.

column.caption: Cortical column — neurons organised into a repeating unit.

mlp.caption: Multilayer perceptron — the same idea, flattened into layers.

attention.caption: Self-attention — every token weighs every other token.

embedding.caption: Embedding space — meaning as distance. Your cursor is the query.

about.heading: Where research meets production.
paragraphs: My work sits between two things I care about: **rigorous machine learning** and **making complex ideas legible**. I've trained models for healthcare decision support — most recently an ensemble that stages sleep from overnight EEG better than its dataset's own published baseline — built a lightweight classifier for astronomical transient detection that holds its own against a full CNN, and authored an IEEE conference paper on contextual similarity matching for chatbots.

Right now most of my research time goes to **D-MT4SR**, a sequential recommender that learns how much each auxiliary item relationship should matter at every step of a user's history rather than fixing one weight for the whole dataset. It beats its published baseline across Amazon benchmarks by a margin that scales with how dense the relation graph is, and the paper is in preparation for IEEE Access.

Before I was writing training pipelines, I was producing how-to guides and marketing videos for AI product teams — which is why I care as much about a clean interface and a clear explanation as I do about a model's F1 score. That combination shapes everything I build.

Outside of coursework and internships, I keep a running list of side projects — from physics-informed networks and CUDA kernels to firmware validation frameworks — mostly to understand a new layer of the stack by building something real in it.
